title: Chapter 9: Multi-Step and Multi-Agent Workflows
content:
Chapter 9: Multi-Step and Multi-Agent Workflows

Opening Hook: More Agents Do Not Automatically Mean Better Results

A single AI assistant can answer a question.

A multi-step AI workflow can plan, research, write, review, and improve an answer.

That sounds powerful.

But there is a trap.

Many beginners think:

If one agent is useful, five agents must be better.

Not always.

More agents can also mean:

  • More cost
  • More latency
  • More confusion
  • More repeated work
  • More hallucination opportunities
  • More difficult debugging

Good multi-agent design is not about adding as many agents as possible.

It is about giving each step a clear job.

In this chapter, you will build your fourth flagship project:

Research and Summary Agent

It will use five role-based steps:

  1. Planner
  2. Researcher
  3. Writer
  4. Reviewer
  5. Reviser

The workflow will take a topic, create a plan, generate careful research notes, write a structured brief, review the brief, and revise it.

This project teaches an important professional pattern:

Complex AI work should be broken into clear, inspectable steps.

What You Will Learn

By the end of this chapter, you will understand:

  • What multi-step AI workflows are
  • What multi-agent workflows are
  • When multiple agents are useful
  • When multiple agents are unnecessary
  • How planner, researcher, writer, reviewer, and reviser roles work
  • How to pass outputs between steps
  • How to save intermediate outputs for debugging
  • How to avoid unsupported research claims
  • How to build a research and summary workflow in Python
  • How to test workflow formatting without making API calls
  • How this pattern applies to business, writing, research, and automation

Why This Chapter Matters

In earlier chapters, you built individual capabilities:

  • LLM calls
  • Command-line apps
  • RAG
  • Semantic search
  • Tool calling
  • Memory
  • Workflow automation

Now you will combine a new idea:

Role-based decomposition.

Instead of asking one model prompt to do everything, you split the task into stages.

A weak single prompt might say:

Research Python AI agents and write a polished article.

That is too broad.

A better workflow says:

Planner: create a research plan. Researcher: create careful notes and mark uncertain claims. Writer: turn notes into a structured brief. Reviewer: identify weak claims, gaps, and unclear sections. Reviser: improve the final brief.

This makes the process easier to inspect and improve.

If the final answer is weak, you can ask:

  • Was the plan weak?
  • Were the notes vague?
  • Did the writer ignore important points?
  • Did the reviewer miss unsupported claims?
  • Did the revision overstate something?

Multi-step workflows make AI systems more controllable.

9.1 What Is a Multi-Step Workflow?

A multi-step workflow is a sequence of tasks where each step has a specific purpose.

Example:

Input topic ↓ Plan ↓ Research notes ↓ Draft ↓ Review ↓ Final output

Each step receives input and produces output.

The output of one step becomes the input for the next step.

This is not necessarily “multi-agent” yet.

It could be one assistant using different prompts.

The value comes from structure.

9.2 What Is a Multi-Agent Workflow?

A multi-agent workflow gives different roles to different AI components.

Each role has its own instruction.

For example:

RoleJob
PlannerDecide what needs to be covered
ResearcherGather or organize notes
WriterCreate the draft
ReviewerCritique the draft
ReviserImprove the final result

In a beginner project, these “agents” may all use the same LLM client with different prompts.

That is fine.

The key idea is role separation.

You do not need a complex agent framework to understand multi-agent design.

You need clear responsibilities.

9.3 Workflow vs Multi-Agent System

These terms can overlap, but here is a simple distinction.

PatternMeaningExample
WorkflowA fixed sequence of stepsPlan → Write → Review
Multi-agent workflowA workflow where each step has a rolePlanner → Researcher → Writer → Reviewer
Fully autonomous agent systemAgents decide more of the process themselvesAgent chooses tools, delegates, loops, stops

This chapter focuses on a controlled multi-agent workflow.

That is the best beginner pattern because it is easier to debug.

9.4 Why Use Multiple Roles?

Multiple roles help because different tasks need different behavior.

A planner should think broadly.

A researcher should be careful.

A writer should be clear.

A reviewer should be critical.

A reviser should improve without adding unsupported claims.

If you ask one prompt to do all of this at once, the output may be shallow.

Role separation forces the model to slow down and focus.

9.5 The Big Warning: This Is Not Verified Web Research

This chapter’s project is called a Research and Summary Agent, but you must understand its limit.

Unless your app is connected to trusted external sources, databases, or approved web search tools, it cannot verify current facts.

The researcher step in this chapter will not browse the web.

It will create structured notes from the model’s existing knowledge and mark claims that need verification.

That means the output is useful for:

  • Brainstorming
  • Planning
  • Drafting
  • Study notes
  • First-pass research structure
  • Content outlines
  • Internal summaries

But it is not enough for:

  • Legal research
  • Medical advice
  • Financial decisions
  • Breaking news
  • Academic citation work
  • Current market claims
  • Publication of factual statistics without verification

A responsible research agent must say when facts need verification.

This chapter includes that rule in the prompts.

9.6 Project: Research and Summary Agent

What This Project Does

This project takes a topic and runs it through a multi-step workflow.

It will produce:

  1. Research plan
  2. Research notes
  3. First draft brief
  4. Review comments
  5. Final revised brief
  6. Saved Markdown report

Who This Helps

This project helps:

  • Students preparing study briefs
  • Writers planning articles
  • Freelancers creating research summaries
  • Founders exploring product ideas
  • Developers building agent workflows
  • Professionals creating internal briefing documents
  • AI builders learning multi-agent orchestration

What You Will Build

Create this project structure:

chapter_09_research_agent/ .env.example .gitignore requirements.txt llm_client.py prompts.py agents.py workflow.py report_writer.py app.py test_prompts.py test_report_writer.py test_workflow_helpers.py README.md

9.7 Setup

Step 1: Create the Folder

mkdir chapter_09_research_agent cd chapter_09_research_agent

Step 2: Create a Virtual Environment

python -m venv .venv

Activate it.

On macOS or Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Step 3: Create requirements.txt

openai python-dotenv

pytest

Install dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4: Create .env.example

OPENAI_API_KEY=replace_with_your_api_key OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2

Copy it to .env.

On macOS or Linux:

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell:

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Then edit .env and add your real API key.

Never publish your real .env file.

9.8 File: .gitignore

Create .gitignore:

.env .venv/ __pycache__/ .pytest_cache/ *.pyc *.log outputs/

9.9 File: llm_client.py

Create llm_client.py:

""" Chapter 9: Reusable LLM Client """

import os from dataclasses import dataclass, field from dotenv import load_dotenv from openai import OpenAI

load_dotenv()

def get_env_float(name: str, default: float) -> float:

"""Read a float from environment variables safely.""" raw_value = os.getenv(name) if raw_value is None: return default try:

return float(raw_value)

except ValueError: return default @dataclass

class LLMConfig:

"""Configuration for the LLM client.""" model: str = field( default_factory=lambda: os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4.1-mini") ) temperature: float = field( default_factory=lambda: get_env_float("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE", 0.2) )

class LLMClient:

"""Small reusable client for sending prompts to an LLM.""" def __init__(self, config: LLMConfig | None = None): self.config = config or LLMConfig() api_key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY") if not api_key: raise ValueError( "OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your .env file." ) self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key) def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str: """Send a request to the model and return text output.""" if not system.strip(): raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.") if not user.strip(): raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.") model_input = f""" System instruction:

{system.strip()}

User request:

{user.strip()}

""" response = self.client.responses.create( model=self.config.model, input=model_input, temperature=self.config.temperature, ) return response.output_text

9.10 File: prompts.py

Create prompts.py:

""" Prompt builders for the Chapter 9 Research and Summary Agent. """ PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """ You are a careful research planner. Your job is to turn a topic into a clear research plan. Do not write the final brief. Do not invent statistics. Focus on useful questions, subtopics, assumptions, and risks. """ RESEARCHER_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """ You are a cautious research note taker. Your job is to create structured research notes based on the provided plan. Do not pretend to browse the web. Do not invent statistics, citations, or sources. Mark any claim that needs verification. Use careful language. """ WRITER_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """ You are a clear technical and business writer. Your job is to turn research notes into a structured brief. Write for beginner-to-intermediate readers. Be practical, clear, and organized. Do not add unsupported facts. """ REVIEWER_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """ You are a strict editor and factual-risk reviewer. Your job is to review a draft for: - Unsupported claims - Vague wording - Missing context - Overpromising - Confusing structure - Claims that need verification Be direct and practical. """ REVISER_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """ You are a careful reviser. Your job is to improve a draft using reviewer feedback. Do not add unsupported facts. Do not add fake citations. Keep the final brief clear, useful, and careful. """

def build_planner_prompt(topic: str) -> str:

"""Build the planner prompt.""" return f""" Create a research plan for this topic:

{topic}

Return: 1. Main research goal 2. Key questions to answer 3. Important subtopics 4. Target reader 5. Practical use cases 6. Risks, assumptions, or unclear areas 7. Suggested final brief structure Important: This is only a plan. Do not write the full brief yet. """

def build_researcher_prompt(topic: str, plan: str) -> str:

"""Build the researcher prompt.""" return f""" Topic:

{topic}

Research plan:

{plan}

Create structured research notes. Return: 1. Key concepts 2. Important context 3. Practical examples 4. Potential benefits 5. Potential risks or limitations 6. Claims that need verification 7. Suggested angles for the final brief Important: - Do not pretend you browsed the web. - Do not invent statistics. - Do not invent citations. - Mark uncertain or current claims as "Needs verification." """

def build_writer_prompt(topic: str, research_notes: str) -> str:

"""Build the writer prompt.""" return f""" Topic:

{topic}

Research notes:

{research_notes}

Write a structured brief. Use this format: # Brief Title ## Executive Summary ## Why This Matters ## Key Ideas ## Practical Use Cases ## Risks and Limitations ## Actionable Recommendations ## Claims to Verify Before Publication Important: - Use clear language. - Do not invent facts. - Do not include fake citations. - Keep the brief practical. """

def build_reviewer_prompt(draft: str) -> str:

"""Build the reviewer prompt.""" return f""" Review the following draft:

{draft}

Return: 1. Strongest parts 2. Weakest parts 3. Unsupported or risky claims 4. Vague sections 5. Missing reader context 6. Suggested improvements 7. Final recommendation: publish, revise, or verify further Be strict but constructive. """

def build_reviser_prompt(draft: str, review: str) -> str:

"""Build the reviser prompt.""" return f""" Original draft:

{draft}

Reviewer feedback:

{review}

Revise the draft. Rules: - Improve clarity and structure. - Remove or soften unsupported claims. - Keep "Claims to Verify Before Publication" if needed. - Do not invent sources or statistics. - Keep the final version practical and publication-friendly. """

9.11 File: agents.py

Create agents.py:

""" Role-based agents for the Chapter 9 Research and Summary Agent. """

from llm_client import LLMClient from prompts import (

PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, RESEARCHER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, WRITER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, REVIEWER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, REVISER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, build_planner_prompt, build_researcher_prompt, build_writer_prompt, build_reviewer_prompt, build_reviser_prompt, )

def planner_agent(topic: str) -> str:

"""Create a research plan.""" client = LLMClient()

return client.complete(

system=PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=build_planner_prompt(topic), )

def researcher_agent(topic: str, plan: str) -> str:

"""Create careful research notes from the plan.""" client = LLMClient()

return client.complete(

system=RESEARCHER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=build_researcher_prompt(topic=topic, plan=plan), )

def writer_agent(topic: str, research_notes: str) -> str:

"""Write a structured brief from research notes.""" client = LLMClient()

return client.complete(

system=WRITER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=build_writer_prompt(topic=topic, research_notes=research_notes), )

def reviewer_agent(draft: str) -> str:

"""Review the draft for clarity and factual risk.""" client = LLMClient()

return client.complete(

system=REVIEWER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=build_reviewer_prompt(draft), )

def reviser_agent(draft: str, review: str) -> str:

"""Revise the draft using reviewer feedback.""" client = LLMClient()

return client.complete(

system=REVISER_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=build_reviser_prompt(draft=draft, review=review), )

9.12 File: workflow.py

Create workflow.py:

""" Workflow orchestration for the Chapter 9 Research and Summary Agent. """

from dataclasses import dataclass

from agents import (

planner_agent, researcher_agent, writer_agent, reviewer_agent, reviser_agent, ) @dataclass

class ResearchWorkflowResult:

"""Stores all outputs from the research workflow.""" topic: str plan: str research_notes: str draft: str review: str final_brief: str

def validate_topic(topic: str) -> str:

""" Validate and clean the research topic. """ cleaned = topic.strip() if not cleaned: raise ValueError("Topic cannot be empty.") if len(cleaned) > 300: raise ValueError("Topic is too long for this beginner demo.") return cleaned

def run_research_workflow(topic: str) -> ResearchWorkflowResult:

""" Run the full planner → researcher → writer → reviewer → reviser workflow. """ cleaned_topic = validate_topic(topic)

print("Step 1/5: Planning...")

plan = planner_agent(cleaned_topic)

print("Step 2/5: Creating research notes...")

research_notes = researcher_agent( topic=cleaned_topic, plan=plan, )

print("Step 3/5: Writing draft brief...")

draft = writer_agent( topic=cleaned_topic, research_notes=research_notes, )

print("Step 4/5: Reviewing draft...")

review = reviewer_agent(draft)

print("Step 5/5: Revising final brief...")

final_brief = reviser_agent( draft=draft, review=review, )

return ResearchWorkflowResult(

topic=cleaned_topic, plan=plan, research_notes=research_notes, draft=draft, review=review, final_brief=final_brief, )

9.13 File: report_writer.py

Create report_writer.py:

""" Markdown report writer for the Chapter 9 Research and Summary Agent. """

from pathlib import Path from datetime import datetime

from workflow import ResearchWorkflowResult

def slugify(text: str, max_length: int = 60) -> str:

""" Create a simple filename-friendly slug. """ allowed = [] for character in text.lower(): if character.isalnum(): allowed.append(character) elif character in {" ", "-", "_"}: allowed.append("_") slug = "".join(allowed) slug = "_".join(part for part in slug.split("_") if part) if not slug: slug = "research_brief"

return slug[:max_length]

def build_markdown_report(result: ResearchWorkflowResult) -> str:

""" Build a Markdown report containing all workflow stages. """ return f"""# Research Workflow Report ## Topic

{result.topic}

--- ## 1. Research Plan

{result.plan}

--- ## 2. Research Notes

{result.research_notes}

--- ## 3. Draft Brief

{result.draft}

--- ## 4. Reviewer Feedback

{result.review}

--- ## 5. Final Revised Brief

{result.final_brief}

--- ## Important Verification Note This workflow does not browse the web or verify current facts by itself. Review factual claims, statistics, legal claims, medical claims, financial claims, and current events before publication or professional use. """

def save_report(

result: ResearchWorkflowResult, output_dir: str = "outputs", ) -> Path: """ Save the workflow report to a Markdown file. """ output_path = Path(output_dir) output_path.mkdir(exist_ok=True) timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S") slug = slugify(result.topic) file_path = output_path / f"{timestamp}_{slug}.md" report = build_markdown_report(result) file_path.write_text(report, encoding="utf-8") return file_path

9.14 File: app.py

Create app.py:

""" Chapter 9 Project: Research and Summary Agent This app runs a multi-step workflow: Planner → Researcher → Writer → Reviewer → Reviser """

from workflow import run_research_workflow from report_writer import save_report

def main() -> None:

"""Run the research and summary workflow."""

print("\nResearch and Summary Agent") print("=" * 45) print("This workflow creates a plan, notes, draft, review, and final brief.") print("It does not verify current facts or browse the web.") print("=" * 45)

topic = input("\nEnter research topic: ").strip() if not topic:

print("No topic provided.")

return try: result = run_research_workflow(topic) report_path = save_report(result)

print("\nFinal Revised Brief") print("=" * 45) print(result.final_brief)

print(f"\nFull workflow report saved to: {report_path}")

except Exception as error:

print(f"\nSomething went wrong: {error}")

if name == "main":

main()

Create test_prompts.py:

from prompts import (

Not executed automatically: requires live API credentials, network access, or external service.

9.18 File: README.md

Create README.md:

````markdown

Project: Research and Summary Agent

This project builds a multi-step AI workflow using role-based agents.

Workflow

Planner → Researcher → Writer → Reviewer → Reviser

Features

  • Creates a research plan
  • Generates cautious research notes
  • Writes a structured brief
  • Reviews the draft for weak claims
  • Revises the final brief
  • Saves all workflow stages to Markdown
  • Includes non-API tests for prompts, reports, and validation

Setup

```text python -m venv .venv

source .venv/bin/activate

pip install -r requirements.txt

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell: python -m venv .venv

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

pip install -r requirements.txt

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Edit `.env` and add your API key. ## Run Tests pytest ## Run the App python app.py ## Example Topics

Python AI agents for freelancers

How RAG improves document assistants

Benefits and risks of AI workflow automation

How small businesses can use AI assistants

## Important Note This workflow does not browse the web or verify current facts by itself. Use it for planning, drafting, learning, and first-pass briefs. Before publishing factual claims, verify them with trusted sources. ## 9.19 How the Code Works This project has five role-based agents. ### Agent 1: Planner The planner receives the topic and creates a research plan. plan = planner_agent(cleaned_topic) The planner does not write the final brief. It defines what should be explored. ### Agent 2: Researcher The researcher receives the topic and plan. research_notes = researcher_agent( topic=cleaned_topic, plan=plan, ) The researcher creates structured notes. The prompt clearly says: Do not pretend you browsed the web. Do not invent statistics. Do not invent citations. Mark uncertain or current claims as "Needs verification." This keeps the workflow more honest. ### Agent 3: Writer The writer receives the research notes and creates a structured brief. draft = writer_agent( topic=cleaned_topic, research_notes=research_notes, ) The writer focuses on clarity and structure. ### Agent 4: Reviewer The reviewer critiques the draft. review = reviewer_agent(draft) The reviewer looks for: Unsupported claims Vague wording Missing context Overpromising Confusing structure Claims that need verification ### Agent 5: Reviser The reviser improves the draft using the review. final_brief = reviser_agent( draft=draft, review=review, ) The final output should be clearer and safer than the first draft. ## 9.20 Why Save Intermediate Outputs? The report includes all stages: Research Plan Research Notes Draft Brief Reviewer Feedback Final Revised Brief This is not just for decoration. It helps you debug. If the final brief is weak, inspect each stage. Maybe the plan was too broad. Maybe the research notes were shallow. Maybe the writer ignored risks. Maybe the reviewer was too gentle. Maybe the reviser added unsupported claims. Saving intermediate outputs makes the workflow easier to improve. In serious AI systems, observability matters. For beginner projects, saving Markdown reports is a simple form of observability. ## 9.21 Sample User Session A typical session may look like this: Research and Summary Agent ============================================= This workflow creates a plan, notes, draft, review, and final brief. It does not verify current facts or browse the web. ============================================= Enter research topic: Python AI agents for freelancers Step 1/5: Planning... Step 2/5: Creating research notes... Step 3/5: Writing draft brief... Step 4/5: Reviewing draft... Step 5/5: Revising final brief... Final Revised Brief ============================================= # Agentic AI With Python for Freelancers ## Executive Summary Python AI agents can help freelancers create practical automation tools... The app also saves a full report: outputs/20260523_142015_python_ai_agents_for_freelancers.md This is sample output only. Do not claim exact output unless you run the code and capture the real result. ## 9.22 Testing the Project Run: pytest Expected type of result: 12 passed The exact number and timing may vary if you add more tests. These tests check: Prompt builders Topic validation Slug generation Markdown report generation The tests do not call the LLM. That is intentional. Multi-step AI workflows can cost more because each run makes several model calls. Test all normal Python logic before running live workflows. ## 9.23 Live API Testing After adding your API key to .env, run: python app.py Try these topics: How RAG helps businesses search internal documents Python AI agents for student productivity Benefits and risks of tool-using AI agents How freelancers can sell AI automation services Review the saved Markdown report. Ask: Is the plan useful? Are the notes careful? Did the draft overpromise? Did the reviewer identify weak claims? Did the final brief improve? This review process is part of building good AI workflows. ## 9.24 Debugging Multi-Step Workflows Multi-step workflows can fail in subtle ways. The best debugging strategy: Inspect the stage before the failure. If the final brief is bad, do not only edit the final prompt. Look at the plan, notes, draft, and review. ## 9.25 When Multi-Agent Workflows Help Multi-agent workflows are helpful when the task has different phases. Good use cases: Research brief creation Proposal development Report writing Content planning Code review Product analysis Customer feedback analysis Business workflow drafting Educational lesson creation They are especially useful when you need a review step. A reviewer role can catch problems the writer role missed. ## 9.26 When Multi-Agent Workflows Are Overkill Do not use multiple agents for everything. Bad use cases: Simple rewriting Short summaries One-line answers Basic classification Small formatting tasks Simple math Tasks that normal Python can handle Example: Convert this title to lowercase. This does not need five agents. Use normal Python: title.lower() A good AI engineer knows when not to use AI. A good agent builder knows when not to use multiple agents. ## 9.27 Cost and Latency Considerations This workflow makes several model calls: Planner call Researcher call Writer call Reviewer call Reviser call That means one user request can become five API calls. This may increase cost and latency. To control cost: Use smaller models for planning or review when possible Limit output length Cache intermediate results Avoid rerunning the whole workflow when only one step needs improvement Save outputs to files Test prompts with short topics first Use multi-step workflows only when they add value For many business apps, a two-step workflow may be enough: Draft → Review or: Analyze → Write Use the simplest workflow that solves the problem. ## 9.28 Adding Tools to This Workflow You can improve this project by adding tools from Chapter 6. For example: ### Search Tool The researcher could call a local knowledge search tool. Researcher → search_notes(topic) ### RAG Tool The researcher could retrieve company documents. Researcher → retrieve_document_chunks(question) ### Calculator Tool The workflow could calculate totals, estimates, or timelines. Planner → calculator("5 * 8") ### Export Tool The final brief could be saved as Markdown, DOCX, or PDF. This creates a more powerful agentic workflow. But always keep tools controlled and observable. ## 9.29 Adding Memory to This Workflow You can improve this project with memory from Chapter 7. Memory could store: The user prefers concise briefs. The user writes for beginner Python learners. The user wants business-focused examples. The user prefers Markdown formatting. Then the writer can adapt the brief. Example flow: Topic ↓ Load relevant memory ↓ Planner creates plan ↓ Researcher creates notes ↓ Writer uses memory preferences ↓ Reviewer checks output This makes the workflow more personal. But do not include irrelevant memory in every step. Too much memory can create noise. ## 9.30 Adding RAG to This Workflow The strongest upgrade is adding RAG. Instead of the researcher relying only on general model knowledge, it can retrieve from approved documents. Example: Topic ↓ Planner creates questions ↓ RAG retrieves relevant source chunks ↓ Researcher summarizes retrieved context ↓ Writer drafts brief ↓ Reviewer checks source support This is more reliable because the workflow has grounded context. A business could use this to generate briefs from: Internal reports Policies Meeting notes Product docs Customer feedback Research libraries That is a strong professional direction for this project. ## 9.31 Real-World Use Case This project can support many real workflows. ### Student Study Briefs Topic: RAG vs fine-tuning Output: Study plan Notes Brief Review Final summary ### Freelancer Research Briefs Topic: AI automation services for small businesses Output: Market angle Service ideas Risks Action plan ### Content Writing Topic: How AI agents use tools Output: Article plan Draft Review Final post ### Business Strategy Topic: How a coaching business can use AI assistants Output: Use cases Benefits Risks Implementation ideas ### Product Planning Topic: Personal document assistant for consultants Output: Problem Users Features Risks MVP plan This project is valuable because it creates structured thinking. ## 9.32 Monetization and Portfolio Angle You can present this project as: Research and Summary Agent Portfolio description: A Python multi-step AI workflow that uses planner, researcher, writer, reviewer, and reviser roles to create structured research briefs while saving intermediate outputs for review and improvement. You are not just calling a model. You are designing a process. ## 9.33 Common Mistakes ### Mistake 1: Using Too Many Agents Do not add agents just because it sounds impressive. Every agent should have a clear job. ### Mistake 2: Giving Agents Overlapping Roles If the researcher writes the full article and the writer rewrites everything, the roles are unclear. Keep roles distinct. ### Mistake 3: Not Saving Intermediate Outputs Without intermediate outputs, debugging is difficult. Save the plan, notes, draft, review, and final result. ### Mistake 4: Pretending the Agent Verified Facts If the workflow did not browse trusted sources, do not say it verified facts. Mark uncertain claims. ### Mistake 5: Skipping the Reviewer The reviewer is one of the most valuable steps. It catches weak claims and unclear writing. ### Mistake 6: Letting the Reviser Add New Claims The reviser should improve the draft, not invent new facts. ### Mistake 7: Ignoring Cost Five model calls cost more than one. Use multi-step workflows where they add real value. ## 9.34 Best Practices Use clear roles. Keep each step focused. Save intermediate outputs. Mark claims that need verification. Use a reviewer step for quality control. Avoid fake citations. Avoid unsupported statistics. Keep workflows as simple as possible. Use RAG for source-grounded research. Use tools only when they add value. Use memory only when relevant. Review final output before publication. ## 9.35 Mini Challenges ### Challenge 1: Add a Critic Score Ask the reviewer to score the draft from 1 to 10 on: clarity usefulness factual risk structure reader fit ### Challenge 2: Add a Short Brief Mode Let the user choose: short medium detailed Then adjust the writer prompt. ### Challenge 3: Add a Source-Grounded Mode Connect Chapter 5 semantic search.
